title: Humans from A to B
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Benjamin Riley interviews Claudio Tennie, a primatologist and cognitive archaeologist at the University of Tübingen, about how humans diverged from an ape-like baseline into a species defined by cultural learning. Tennie argues that the decisive capacity is copying, which humans do effortlessly and great apes essentially do not, and he sets out three criteria that genuine copying must satisfy: resemblance, causal dependence, and the learner doing something beyond their own latent repertoire. His experiments, including a trained chimpanzee whose banana-earning gesture no other chimp imitated, show apes failing the third test. Tennie's zone of latent solutions theory suggests that early stone tools, long assumed to be cultural, may have been reinvented independently, which pushes the start of human copying to roughly 800,000 years ago. The conversation connects copying to language and skilled trades, and closes with Tennie describing large language models as compressed culture machines that still regurgitate the biases of their training data.
points: Tennie's three criteria for true copying are resemblance, a causal link between demonstration and output, and the learner doing something beyond what they could develop alone.
Most ape imitation experiments fail the third criterion because they test behaviors apes already produce spontaneously, which shows triggering rather than copying.
The near-identical form of early stone tools across huge spans of time and distance suggests they did not depend on copying at all.
Language requires copying, so any skill that depends on language, such as elaborate carpentry traditions, inherits that dependence.
Tennie describes AI models as compressed, distilled versions of culture and judges that they will matter most if they learn to counteract their own biases like real scientists.
quotes: There are many factors to get human language off the ground, but one of the necessary ones is the ability to copy from others, and copy how things are communicated. We learn this from the culture around us, from the usage of words and signs by others.

And what I noticed, as others before me, is that the earliest stone tools essentially stayed the same for hundreds of thousands of years, and they look very similar across thousands of kilometers of distance, and they even stay similiar across presumable environmental changes and even across hominin species.

Not just doing something different, but doing something that goes beyond what they normally do, or could develop on their own, even if they were very motivated. This third factor is where most existing experiments fail. Many ape experiments test ape learners after giving them tasks that were within their existing capabilities, thus failing to test for this third factor.
I have trained apes to perform forms of behavior or tasks that they wouldn’t perform on their own. It’s painstaking work, it takes a long time, but these studies can be done.

For us, we don’t even think about it. When you want to make a class of kindergarteners happy, you go in and play silly imitation games. They love them, and they are very good at playing them from a young age.
Language requires copying. That’s not a new thought, others have said this too. And copying is not the only thing that is required here.
That we are now essentially producing culture machines. It’s not a perfect term, but what is being created at the moment are compressed, distilled versions of our culture, essentially.
I am more interested in whether they can be evolved (or can evolve) to act as real scientists, that is, by counteracting their biases.
